standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 4.3.5 (Overfitting with a Nonlinear CEF), the CEF identity, corrected ($g(x)$ for $g(X)$)
canonical_claim.location: p. 163 (PDF p. 181), Example 4.3.5, first two sentences
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Example 4.3.5. Overfitting with a Nonlinear CEF. Suppose we had a random vector $(X, Y)$ such that $Y = g(X) + \varepsilon$, for some (nonlinear) function $g$, where $X \sim U(-10, 10)$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 25)$, and $X \perp\!\!\!\perp \varepsilon$. The CEF of $Y$ given $X$ is thus $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = g(X)$. Let $g$ be the function shown in black in Figure 4.3.4. [Corrected statement] ... The CEF of $Y$ given $X$ is thus $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = g(x)$. Let $g$ be the function shown in black in Figure 4.3.5. [Formal content] Let $X$ and $\varepsilon$ be independent random variables with $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$, let $g$ be a function of $X$ with $\mathrm{E}|g(X)| < \infty$, and let $Y = g(X) + \varepsilon$. Then $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = g(x)$ for all $x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$; equivalently $\mathrm{E}[Y|X] = g(X)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Theorem 2.2.14, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] Linearity of Conditional Expectations. For random variables $X$ and $Y$, if $g$ and $h$ are functions of $X$, then $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $\mathrm{E}[g(X)Y + h(X)|X = x] = g(x)\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] + h(x)$. [Theorem 2.2.25, p. 82 (PDF p. 100)] If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then $\mathrm{E}[Y|X] = \mathrm{E}[Y]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $G_Y(X)$, where $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: statistical; confirmed in part). The finding has two parts. Part (a), the model labels of Figure 4.4.4 (panels (6)–(8) omit the pure power terms that Table 4.4.5 lists, and a subscript is set on the baseline in panel (4)), is a labelling of regression specifications in a figure of the application, with no mathematical statement to correct, and is not a target. Part (b) is the identity above: the printed right-hand side $g(X)$ is a random variable where the left-hand side is a function of the fixed value $x$, and the figure reference should be to Figure 4.3.5. The corrected identity follows from Theorems 2.2.14 and 2.2.25.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 4.3.8 (Differences between the Average Partial Derivative and the Partial Derivative at the Average), with the subscripts of the two displays corrected; and the label in the sentence after Definition 4.3.6
canonical_claim.location: Example 4.3.8: p. 167 (PDF p. 185). Sentence after Definition 4.3.6: p. 166 (PDF p. 184). Definitions 4.3.6 and 4.3.7: pp. 166–167
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement, p. 167] Example 4.3.8. Suppose $X_{[1]} \perp\!\!\!\perp X_{[2]}$ with $X_{[1]} \sim U(0, 1)$ and $X_{[2]} \sim U(0, 1)$. Further suppose that the CEF is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}] = -X_{[1]}$ if $X_{[2]} \le .8$, and $9X_{[1]}$ if $X_{[2]} > .8$. Then, by the Law of Iterated Expectations, $APD_{X_{[1]}} = \frac{\partial(-X_{[1]})}{\partial X_{[1]}}\Pr[X_{[2]} \le .8] + \frac{\partial(9X_{[1]})}{\partial X_{[1]}}\Pr[X_{[2]i} > .8] = -1 \times .8 + 9 \times .2 = 1$. But the partial derivative at the average gives a very different result: $PDA_{X_{[k]}} = \frac{\partial(-X_{[1]})}{\partial X_{[1]}} = -1$. While the partial derivative with respect to $X_{[1]}$ is positive on average, when evaluated at the average ($X_{[1]} = X_{[2]} = 0.5$), the partial derivative is negative. [p. 166] A natural plug-in estimator for $APD_{X_{[k]i}}$ is obtained by replacing the expected value with a sample mean and the CEF with the estimated CEF: $\widehat{APD}_{X_{[k]}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\left.\frac{\partial\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}_i}\right)$. [Corrected displays] $APD_{X_{[1]}} = \frac{\partial(-X_{[1]})}{\partial X_{[1]}}\Pr[X_{[2]} \le .8] + \frac{\partial(9X_{[1]})}{\partial X_{[1]}}\Pr[X_{[2]} > .8] = -1 \times .8 + 9 \times .2 = 1$; $PDA_{X_{[1]}} = \frac{\partial(-X_{[1]})}{\partial X_{[1]}} = -1$. [p. 166] A natural plug-in estimator for $APD_{X_{[k]}}$ is obtained by ... [Formal content] Let $X_{[1]} \perp\!\!\!\perp X_{[2]}$ with $X_{[1]} \sim U(0, 1)$ and $X_{[2]} \sim U(0, 1)$, and let $m(x_1, x_2) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X_{[1]} = x_1, X_{[2]} = x_2] = -x_1$ for $x_2 \le .8$ and $9x_1$ for $x_2 > .8$. Then $\frac{\partial m}{\partial x_1}(x_1, x_2) = -1$ for $x_2 \le .8$ and $9$ for $x_2 > .8$; $APD_{X_{[1]}} = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial m}{\partial x_1}(X_{[1]}, X_{[2]})\right] = -1 \times \frac{8}{10} + 9 \times \frac{2}{10} = 1$; $\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}] = (\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})$ and $PDA_{X_{[1]}} = \frac{\partial m}{\partial x_1}(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) = -1$. So $APD_{X_{[1]}} \ne PDA_{X_{[1]}}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Definition 4.3.6, p. 166] Average Partial Derivative. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$, the average partial derivative of the CEF (of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X}$) with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $APD_{X_{[k]}} = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right]$. [Definition 4.3.7, p. 167] Partial Derivative at the Average. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$, the partial derivative at the average of the CEF (of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X}$) with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $PDA_{X_{[k]}} = \left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]}$. [p. 166] the partial derivative of the CEF with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $\left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}}$. [Example 1.2.18, p. 28 (PDF p. 46)] $U(0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo; confirmed in part): a stray observation index in $\Pr[X_{[2]i} > .8]$, the generic label $PDA_{X_{[k]}}$ on a display that differentiates with respect to $X_{[1]}$, and $APD_{X_{[k]i}}$ on p. 166; the validator records these as labelling slips, the arithmetic ($APD = 1$, $PDA = -1$) being right. The example is the formal content of headline claim P001-ch04-H7 (the APD and the PDA differ in general), which held up. Here the mean $(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})$ is an interior point of the support, so the PDA is well defined (compare the Moderate finding P001-C04-E002).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.9 (Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator), the least squares criterion, corrected (the missing square)
canonical_claim.location: p. 169 (PDF p. 187), the display defining $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ (the definition begins on p. 168, PDF p. 186)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed display] $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_n+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J_n} b_kX_i^k\right)$, where $J_n \to \infty$ and $\frac{1}{n}J_n \to 0$. [Corrected display] $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_n+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J_n} b_kX_i^k\right)^2$. [Formal content] For any real data $(y_i, x_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$ and any $J \ge 0$: (i) the printed criterion $\mathbf{b} \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J} b_kx_i^k\right)$ is unbounded below (it equals $\sum_i y_i - nb_0 - \sum_{k \ge 1} b_k\sum_i x_i^k$, which tends to $-\infty$ as $b_0 \to \infty$ with the other coefficients fixed), so it has no minimizer; (ii) the corrected criterion is the sum of squared residuals of the regression of $Y$ on $(1, X, X^2, ..., X^J)$; when the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ with rows $(1, x_i, ..., x_i^J)$ has $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$ invertible (which requires at least $J + 1$ distinct values among the $x_i$), its unique minimizer is $(\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{y}$ (Theorem 4.1.4).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Definition 4.3.9, p. 168] the polynomial least squares sieve estimator of the conditional expectation function is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x] = \sum_{k=0}^{J_n}\hat\beta_kx^k$. [Theorem 4.1.4, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] if $\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X}$ is invertible, the OLS coefficient estimator is $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{Y}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): the exponent 2 is missing from the residual; the estimator's name and the text make least squares evident. The validator notes that the unsquared criterion is unbounded below for every nonempty sample. Restoring the square does not validate the printed rate condition, which is the separate Moderate finding P001-C04-E001.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.10 (Lasso Estimator), corrected: the coefficient vector in $\mathbb{R}^{K+1}$ and the penalty on the slope coefficients
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Definition 4.3.10. Lasso Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ where $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$, the lasso estimator with penalty parameter $\lambda$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^K}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{b})^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{b}\|_1\right)$, where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the $\ell^1$ norm, that is, $\|\mathbf{b}\|_1 = \sum_{k=1}^{K}|b_k|$ (the sum of the absolute value of the coefficients). [Corrected statement] Definition 4.3.10. Lasso Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ where $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$, the lasso estimator with penalty parameter $\lambda$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{b})^2 + \lambda\sum_{k=1}^{K}|b_k|\right]$, where $\mathbf{b} = (b_0, b_1, ..., b_K)^T$, $b_0$ is the unpenalized intercept, and the penalty is $\lambda$ times the $\ell^1$ norm of the slope subvector $(b_1, ..., b_K)$. [Statement attached to the definition, p. 170, as printed] If we let $\lambda = 0$, then the lasso is equivalent to regular OLS regression. [Formal content] (i) $\mathbf{X}_i = (1, X_{[1]i}, ..., X_{[K]i})$ has $K + 1$ components, so $\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{b}$ is defined for $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}$ and not for $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^K$. (ii) $\mathbf{b} \mapsto \sum_{k=1}^{K}|b_k|$ is a seminorm on $\mathbb{R}^{K+1}$ and is not the $\ell^1$ norm of $\mathbf{b}$ (it vanishes at $(1, 0, ..., 0)$). (iii) For $\lambda = 0$ the corrected criterion is $\frac{1}{n}$ times the OLS sum of squared residuals of Definition 4.1.2, so $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0$ is the OLS coefficient estimator whenever that is unique. (iv) For every $\lambda \ge 0$ the corrected criterion is a convex function of $\mathbf{b}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [p. 169] The key for the lasso is that the penalty term is the sum of the absolute value of estimated regression coefficients (typically excluding the intercept). [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165)] the OLS coefficient estimator minimizes $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$ over $(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): the arg min is taken over $\mathbb{R}^K$ for a $(K + 1)$-vector, and '$\ell^1$ norm' is used for the slope-only penalty. This is a correction to a definition; the provable content is (i)–(iv). Part of headline claim P001-ch04-H9 (the lasso 'equals OLS at $\lambda = 0$'). The asymptotic remark on p. 170 (consistency when $\lambda \to 0$ with $K$ fixed and a linear CEF) is stated in the book without proof and is not transcribed as a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 5.1.4 (Classical Linear Model), the parameter space, corrected ($\sigma > 0$); with Theorem 5.1.5 (CEF of the Classical Linear Model)
canonical_claim.location: Definition 5.1.4: pp. 180–181 (PDF pp. 198–199). Theorem 5.1.5: p. 181 (PDF p. 199)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Definition 5.1.4. Classical Linear Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$, the classical linear model is a parametric model with $g(y, \mathbf{x}; (\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma)) = \phi(y; (\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2))$, where $\boldsymbol\beta = (\beta_0, \beta_1, ..., \beta_K)^T$, $\phi(y; (\mu, \sigma^2))$ denotes the PDF of the normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, and the parameter space is $\boldsymbol\Theta = \{(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+2} : \sigma \ge 0\}$. [Corrected parameter space] $\boldsymbol\Theta = \{(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+2} : \sigma > 0\}$. [Theorem 5.1.5, p. 181, as printed; unchanged] CEF of the Classical Linear Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X} = (1, X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]})$, if the classical linear model is true, then the CEF of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X}$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$. [Formal content] (i) For $\sigma > 0$, $\phi(y; (\mu, \sigma^2)) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$ is a PDF in $y$ with mean $\mu$; at $\sigma = 0$ the expression is undefined (Definition 2.1.19 requires $\sigma > 0$), so $g(y, \mathbf{x}; (\boldsymbol\beta, 0))$ is not a member of the model. (ii) Theorem 5.1.5: if $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = \phi(y; (\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2))$ for some $(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma)$ with $\sigma > 0$, then $\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y\phi(y; (\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2))dy = \mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] Parametric Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 2.1.19, p. 55 (PDF p. 73)] the normal PDF $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$ for constants $\mu, \sigma \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\sigma > 0$. [Theorem 2.1.20, p. 56 (PDF p. 74)] If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and $\sigma[X] = \sigma$. [Definition 2.3.3, p. 85 (PDF p. 103)] for jointly continuous $X_{[1]}, ..., X_{[K]}$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})dy$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): the parameter space is printed with $\sigma \ge 0$ where the normal density needs $\sigma > 0$. The target also carries the first part of headline claim P001-ch05-H1 (if the classical linear model is true the CEF is $\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta$), which held up. $\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta$ is the product of the row vector $\mathbf{x} = (1, x_{[1]}, ..., x_{[K]})$ and the column vector $\boldsymbol\beta$.
